title: Herod the Great
summary: The Rome-appointed king of Judea whose paranoia met the nativity — the tyrant at the threshold of the gospel.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Herod "the Great," the Rome-appointed king of Judea, appears in Matthew's nativity: told by the magi that a king of the Jews has been born, he feigns worship, then — outwitted — orders the massacre of the boys of Bethlehem, from which the child Jesus escapes into Egypt (Matthew 2). He is the tyrant at the threshold of the gospel.

**What history confirms.** Herod is one of the best-documented figures of the era: the historian Josephus devotes pages to his brutal, brilliant reign (37–4 BC), and his colossal building works survive — the rebuilt Jerusalem temple, the fortress-palaces of Masada and the Herodium, the harbor city of Caesarea. Marked *attested*. His death in 4 BC is one anchor that places Jesus' birth slightly earlier. The Bethlehem massacre itself is unattested outside Matthew, but it fits all that is known of Herod's paranoia — he executed his own wife and sons.

**His place in the story.** Herod is the first of several rulers — Herod, Pilate, later the emperors — before whom the gospel stands on trial; the newborn king meets the reigning king, and power recognizes a rival.
readingPointer: His part in the nativity is told in Matthew 2.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on Matthew 2
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Herod"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years

title: Mary
summary: The mother of Jesus, whose "let it be to me" and Magnificat make her the first and model disciple — and the most honored, and most disputed, woman in Christian tradition.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Mary, a young woman of Nazareth betrothed to Joseph, is greeted by the angel Gabriel: she will bear a son, conceived by the Holy Spirit, and call him Jesus (Luke 1:26–38). Her answer — "let it be to me according to your word" — and her song, the Magnificat ("my soul magnifies the Lord… he has exalted the humble," Luke 1:46–55), make her the first and model disciple. She bears Jesus, presents him in the temple (where Simeon warns that a sword will pierce her own soul), stands at the foot of the cross where the dying Jesus gives her into John's care (John 19:25–27), and is among the disciples at Pentecost (Acts 1:14).

**Register and dating.** Mary is known historically only through the Gospels; her dates are traditional. Marked *traditional*.

**Where the traditions differ.** Mary is honored across all Christian traditions — but *how* differs sharply, over her perpetual virginity, her conception, her assumption, and prayer to her. The views are set side by side below, none endorsed.
readingPointer: Read the Annunciation and Magnificat in Luke 1.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on Luke 1–2
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Mary, the Blessed Virgin"

traditions.catholic: Catholic teaching honors Mary as ever-virgin, Mother of God (Theotokos), conceived without original sin (the Immaculate Conception, defined 1854), and assumed body and soul into heaven (1950); she is venerated and asked for her intercession — honor (hyperdulia) distinct from the worship due to God alone.
traditions.orthodox: Orthodoxy venerates Mary as Theotokos and Ever-Virgin, central to its worship and icons, holding her supreme holiness and her Dormition ("falling asleep"); but it frames sin and grace differently and does not define the Immaculate Conception in the Roman manner.
traditions.protestant: Protestant traditions honor Mary as the blessed, faithful mother of the Lord and treasure the Magnificat, but reject the later Marian doctrines (immaculate conception, bodily assumption) as lacking scriptural warrant, and reject prayer to Mary — reserving worship and mediation for Christ alone.

title: Joseph of Nazareth
summary: The carpenter of David's line who took Mary as his wife and gave Jesus his name and legal descent — the last link of the gold thread.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Joseph, a carpenter (Greek *tekton*) of Nazareth and "a just man" of David's line, is betrothed to Mary; finding her with child he resolves to divorce her quietly, until an angel tells him the child is of the Holy Spirit, and he takes Mary as his wife and names the boy Jesus (Matthew 1:18–25). He shelters the family in the flight to Egypt and the return to Nazareth (Matthew 2), and appears last when Jesus is twelve (Luke 2); tradition holds he died before Jesus' public ministry.

**Register and dating.** Joseph is known only through the Gospels; marked *traditional*.

**On the line of promise.** It is *through Joseph* that Matthew traces the royal line of David to Jesus (Matthew 1:16), which is why the gold thread reaches its end through him — and yet Matthew's wording shifts deliberately at the last link: not "Joseph the father of Jesus" but "Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born." Joseph gives Jesus his legal Davidic descent and his name; the conception, the Gospels confess, is of the Holy Spirit. (Matthew's and Luke's genealogies differ, and how to reconcile them — whether Luke traces Mary's line, or Joseph's by another route — is an old and open question this project notes rather than settles.)
readingPointer: His part is told in Matthew 1–2.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on Matthew 1–2
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Joseph, St"

title: Annunciation & Nativity
summary: The angel to Mary, and the birth at Bethlehem — where the promise threaded from Abraham and David arrives as a child.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Two Gospels tell of Jesus' birth. Luke gives the Annunciation — Gabriel to Mary — the journey to Bethlehem for a census, the birth laid in a manger "because there was no place for them in the inn," and the angels and shepherds (Luke 1–2). Matthew gives Joseph's dream, the magi from the east following a star, Herod's plot, and the flight to Egypt (Matthew 1–2). Both name Bethlehem, the city of David, echoing Micah 5:2, and both affirm the virgin conception "of the Holy Spirit."

**Register and history.** That Jesus was born, late in Herod's reign (c. 6–4 BC), is history; the theological heart of the narratives — the virgin birth, the incarnation of the Word — is the confession of scripture and creed, which history can neither prove nor disprove. Some details are debated: the census under Quirinius (Luke 2:2) is hard to square with the known chronology, a genuine difficulty scholars discuss. This entry is marked *traditional*, holding the register with care.

**Its meaning.** "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). The nativity is the hinge of the whole timeline — where the promise threaded through Abraham and David arrives as a child, and, in Christian confession, God enters his own creation.
readingPointer: Read the nativity in Luke 2 and Matthew 2.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on Luke 1–2 and Matthew 1–2
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Nativity of Christ"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years

title: Jesus Christ
summary: The one the gospels proclaim as Messiah and Lord — the figure in whom the line of promise arrives.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** The gospels tell of a birth in Bethlehem in the days of Herod, a hidden youth in Nazareth, a public ministry of announcement — "the kingdom of God is at hand" (Mark 1:15) — with teaching, healing, and the calling of twelve disciples; then a final Passover in Jerusalem, crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, and, on the third day, the resurrection the whole New Testament stands on. Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy this canvas draws in gold: "Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1) — the line of promise arriving at its destination.

**What history can say.** That Jesus of Nazareth lived and was crucified under Pontius Pilate is about as well-established as ancient history gets: besides the New Testament documents themselves (the earliest within a generation of the events), the Roman historian Tacitus (*Annals* 15.44) and the Jewish historian Josephus (*Antiquities* 18 and 20 — the famous passage partly reworked by later copyists, but its core widely accepted) both attest him. The framing dates are approximate: born c. 6–4 BC (before Herod the Great's death in 4 BC — the calendar's misalignment is a sixth-century computational artifact), crucified at Passover in either AD 30 or 33, the two candidates the evidence supports.

**Where the registers part.** History can attest a crucified teacher; the resurrection and the confession "my Lord and my God" (John 20:28) are claims of a different order, which historians as historians can neither certify nor forbid. This project states plainly that the church's confession — Messiah, Lord, risen — is the scriptural and creedal register speaking, presents it fairly, and leaves the reader before the question the gospels intend to pose.
readingPointer: Start with the Gospel of Mark — the shortest and swiftest of the four.
sources: ESV Study Bible, introductions to the Gospels
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Jesus Christ"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years
Henry Chadwick, The Early Church

title: John the Baptist
summary: The wilderness prophet who baptized Jesus and pointed beyond himself — "Behold, the Lamb of God" — the hinge between the Testaments.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** John, son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth (Mary's kinswoman), is born to aged parents (Luke 1) and grows into a prophet in the wilderness — camel's hair, locusts and wild honey — preaching repentance and a baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and pointing beyond himself: "Behold, the Lamb of God" (John 1:29). He baptizes Jesus in the Jordan (Matthew 3), and is later beheaded by Herod Antipas for denouncing the ruler's marriage (Mark 6).

**What history confirms.** John is independently attested: Josephus describes him (*Antiquities* 18.5.2) as a good man who baptized and was executed by Herod Antipas — one of the era's firmest external confirmations of a Gospel figure. Marked *attested*.

**His place in the story.** John is the hinge between the Testaments — "the voice of one crying in the wilderness" (Isaiah 40:3) — the last of the old prophets and the forerunner the church identifies with the returning Elijah (Matthew 11:14). Jesus calls him the greatest born of women.
readingPointer: Read his ministry and the baptism of Jesus in Matthew 3.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on the Gospels
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "John the Baptist, St"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years

title: Pontius Pilate
summary: The Roman prefect who condemned Jesus and washed his hands — the name that fixes the gospel in datable history.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Pontius Pilate, the Roman prefect of Judea, is the judge at Jesus' trial: he finds no guilt in him, tries to release him, has him flogged, washes his hands before the crowd — "I am innocent of this man's blood" (Matthew 27:24) — and yet, fearing unrest and Caesar's displeasure, hands him over to be crucified, fixing the charge above the cross: "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews" (John 19:19).

**What history confirms.** Pilate is firmly historical: he governed Judea AD 26–36, is described by Josephus, Philo, and Tacitus (who names him in connection with Christ's execution), and an inscription bearing his name — the "Pilate Stone" — was found at Caesarea in 1961. Marked *attested*. His role makes the crucifixion one of the best-anchored events of the era.

**His place in the story.** Pilate's name enters the creed — Jesus "suffered under Pontius Pilate" — fixing the gospel in datable, Roman history: not "once upon a time" but under a named governor, in a known reign.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on the Passion narratives
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Pilate, Pontius"
Diarmaid MacCulloch, Christianity: The First Three Thousand Years

title: Baptism of Jesus
summary: Jesus baptized by John in the Jordan — the Spirit as a dove, the Father's voice, the opening of his ministry.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Jesus comes to John at the Jordan and is baptized; as he rises from the water, the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice declares, "You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased" (Mark 1:9–11). It opens his public ministry, and the Gospels present it as the moment the Trinity is disclosed — the Father's voice, the Spirit's descent, the Son in the water.

**Register and history.** That Jesus was baptized by John is regarded by historians as among the most secure facts about him (why would the movement invent its Lord submitting to John's baptism of repentance?). Marked *attested*. The theophany — the voice, the descending Spirit — is the confession of the Gospels.

**Its meaning.** Jesus, needing no repentance, takes his place with sinners in the sinners' baptism — the first act of a ministry that will end taking their place at the cross.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on the Gospels
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Baptism of Christ"

title: Public Ministry & the Sermon on the Mount
summary: Three years of the kingdom announced — parables, healings, the calling of the twelve, and the Beatitudes.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** For some three years Jesus travels Galilee and Judea announcing the kingdom of God — teaching in parables, healing the sick, casting out demons, eating with tax collectors and sinners, and calling twelve disciples. The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) gathers the heart of his teaching: the Beatitudes ("Blessed are the poor in spirit…"), love of enemies, the Lord's Prayer, "do not be anxious," the golden rule — a vision of life in the kingdom that has shaped ethics far beyond the church.

**Register and history.** That Jesus was an itinerant teacher and healer with a following is attested (Tacitus, Josephus); the specific content — the Sermon, the parables — comes from the Gospels, which most scholars agree preserve the substance of a genuinely distinctive teacher. Marked *attested* for the ministry, with the teaching held in the scriptural register.

**Its reach.** The Sermon on the Mount alone has moved Augustine, Francis, Tolstoy, Gandhi, and Martin Luther King Jr. — a text whose demands the church has never finished reckoning with.
readingPointer: Read the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5–7.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on the Gospels
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Sermon on the Mount"

title: The Transfiguration
summary: Jesus shining on the mountain between Moses and Elijah — a glimpse of glory before the road to the cross.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** On a high mountain, before Peter, James, and John, Jesus is transfigured — his face and clothes shining with light — and Moses and Elijah appear speaking with him; a cloud overshadows them and the Father's voice repeats, "This is my beloved Son; listen to him" (Mark 9:2–8). It is a glimpse of glory midway through the ministry, set between the first prediction of the passion and the road to Jerusalem.

**Register.** The Transfiguration is a scriptural and theological event — a disclosure of Christ's glory — not one external history can corroborate (marked *traditional*).

**Its meaning.** Moses (the Law) and Elijah (the Prophets) flank Jesus and then fade, leaving him alone: the whole Old Testament, the church reads, pointing to him and handing over to him. 2 Peter recalls being "with him on the holy mountain" (2 Peter 1:16–18).
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on the Gospels
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Transfiguration"

title: The Triumphal Entry
summary: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey to shouts of Hosanna — a humble king, opening the last week.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Jesus enters Jerusalem for the last Passover riding a donkey, and the crowds spread cloaks and palm branches, shouting "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" (Mark 11:1–10) — a deliberate, humble fulfillment of Zechariah's king coming "lowly and riding on a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9). The church keeps it as Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week.

**Register.** The entry is narrated in all four Gospels and kept in tradition (marked *traditional*); it opens the passion — the most historically anchored week of Jesus' life.

**Its meaning.** The crowd hails a king it expects to drive out Rome; within days it will call for his death. Jesus enters not on a war-horse but a donkey — claiming kingship, and redefining it.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on the Gospels
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Palm Sunday"

title: The Last Supper
summary: The Passover meal where Jesus gave bread and cup as his body and blood — "do this in remembrance of me."
article:
**What scripture narrates.** On the night he is betrayed, Jesus keeps the Passover with his disciples, washes their feet, and takes bread and wine: "This is my body… this is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many" (Mark 14:22–24), commanding, "Do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19). He foretells his betrayal and Peter's denial, and gives the new commandment to love one another (John 13–17). It is the origin of the church's central rite — the Eucharist, the Lord's Supper, Holy Communion.

**Register.** Narrated in the Gospels and in Paul's even earlier account (1 Corinthians 11:23–26), and kept in unbroken tradition (marked *traditional*).

**Where the traditions differ.** *What happens* in the Supper — how Christ is present in the bread and wine — is among the most divisive questions in Christian history (transubstantiation, real presence, spiritual presence, memorial). This project flags the dispute; it belongs more fully to the Reformation entries where it erupted.
readingPointer: Read the supper in Luke 22 and John 13.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on the Gospels
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Eucharist"

title: The Crucifixion
summary: Jesus crucified under Pilate at Golgotha — Rome's most shameful execution, which the church reads as the center of everything.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** Betrayed by Judas, denied by Peter, condemned by the council and by Pilate, Jesus is flogged, mocked with a crown of thorns, and crucified at Golgotha between two criminals; he prays for his executioners, cries out, and dies, and is buried in a new tomb (Mark 15). The Gospels present it not as defeat but as the purpose of his coming — "the Son of Man came… to give his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).

**What history confirms.** The crucifixion of Jesus under Pontius Pilate is about as certain as anything in ancient history: Tacitus states it plainly (*Annals* 15.44), Josephus attests it, and Paul proclaims it within two decades. Crucifixion was Rome's most shameful execution — a fact so damaging to a new movement that its very centrality is itself a kind of evidence. Marked *attested*.

**Where the registers meet.** History attests a man crucified; *why* it happened — sin borne, a ransom paid, the world reconciled — is the confession of the New Testament, which reads the cross as the center of everything. The many ways the church has understood the atonement are held here, not resolved.
readingPointer: Read the crucifixion in Mark 15 or John 19.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on the Passion narratives
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Crucifixion" and "Atonement"
Henry Chadwick, The Early Church

title: The Resurrection
summary: The empty tomb and the appearances of the risen Jesus — the ground the whole New Testament stands on, and the timeline's most register-sensitive entry.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** On the third day, the tomb is found empty, and the risen Jesus appears — to Mary Magdalene, to the disciples behind locked doors, to two on the Emmaus road, to Thomas, and, Paul reports, to more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). The resurrection is the ground the entire New Testament stands on: "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile" (1 Corinthians 15:17).

**Where the registers part — carefully.** This is the most register-sensitive entry on the timeline. What history can weigh: that Jesus' followers, scattered and devastated by the crucifixion, within weeks were proclaiming him risen and dying for that claim; that the tomb was reported empty; that the movement exploded from that conviction. What history *cannot* do, as history, is certify or forbid a bodily resurrection — a claim of a different order. This entry is marked *traditional*: it is the church's central confession, presented plainly and fairly, neither dressed up as neutral fact nor explained away. The reader is left before exactly the question the Gospels intend.

**Its meaning.** For the New Testament the resurrection is God's vindication of the crucified — the firstfruits of a promised new creation, and the reason there is a church at all.
readingPointer: Read the resurrection in Luke 24 and John 20.
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on the Resurrection narratives
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Resurrection of Christ"
Henry Chadwick, The Early Church

title: The Ascension
summary: The risen Jesus taken up into a cloud, with the great commission and the promise of return — the story handed to the church.
article:
**What scripture narrates.** After forty days of resurrection appearances, Jesus leads his disciples out, commissions them — "you will be my witnesses… to the end of the earth" — and is taken up into a cloud, with the promise that he will return as he went (Acts 1:6–11; Luke 24:50–53). It is the last of the earthly events of Jesus' life and the threshold of the church's.

**Register.** The Ascension is narrated in scripture and confessed in the creeds ("he ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father"); it is a theological claim about Christ's exaltation, not an event external history records (marked *traditional*).

**Its meaning.** The Ascension hands the story to the church: the risen Lord withdraws his visible presence and, at Pentecost, pours out his Spirit — where this canvas's biblical story opens into the age of the church. It is also the hinge of hope: the same Jesus "will come in the same way."
sources: ESV Study Bible, notes on Acts 1
The Oxford Dictionary of the Christian Church, "Ascension"
